US Hazards Outlook
NWS Climate Prediction Center College Park MD
300 PM EST November 13 2026

SYNOPSIS: Mid-level low pressure is forecast to extend from the Aleutians 
southeastward to the West Coast during mid to late November. A stormy pattern 
is likely from the Rockies across the central and east-central Contiguous U.S. 
(CONUS) during the first half of week-2, with the storm activity shifting to 
the West Coast during the second half. The enhanced Pacific flow favors mostly 
near to above normal temperatures across the CONUS. Below normal temperatures 
are slightly favored for much of the southwestern quarter of the CONUS during 
week-2, with portions of the Southern Plains expected to see their first freeze 
of the season. Warmer than normal temperatures continue to be favored for 
Alaska, with near to above normal precipitation for the state.

HAZARDS

Slight risk of heavy precipitation for much of the eastern Plains and 
Mississippi Valley, Upper Great Lakes region, and western portions of the Ohio 
and Tennessee Valleys, and Southeastern CONUS, Sat-Sun, Nov 21-22.

Slight risk of heavy precipitation for northern California and southwestern 
Oregon, Wed-Fri, Nov 25-27.

Slight risk of heavy snow for portions of the central Rockies and adjacent 
parts of the central High Plains (including the Front Range area), Sat-Sun, Nov 
21-22.

Slight risk of heavy snow for higher elevations of the Klamath and northern 
Sierra Nevada Mountains, Wed-Fri, Nov 25-27.

Slight risk of much below normal temperatures (and possible first freeze) for 
much of the Southern Plains and parts of adjacent states, Tue-Wed, Nov 24-25.

Slight risk of high winds for much of the country between the Rockies and 
Appalachians, Sat-Tue, Nov 21-24.

Slight risk of high winds for northern California and southwestern Oregon, 
Wed-Fri, Nov 25-27.

DETAILED SUMMARY

FOR MONDAY NOVEMBER 16 - FRIDAY NOVEMBER 20: 
https://www.wpc.ncep.noaa.gov/threats/threats.php

FOR SATURDAY NOVEMBER 21 - FRIDAY NOVEMBER 27: Early in week-2, a mid-level 
trough is predicted to move across the Four Corners region and into the Great 
Plains. During this time, lee cyclogenesis is forecast in the general vicinity 
of southeast Colorado. The GEFS and ECENS disagree on the predicted track of 
this surface low, with the GEFS favoring a northeastward path towards the 
Arrowhead of Minnesota, while the ECENS favors an eastward track into the 
Midwest. North of the surface low, easterly flow is anticipated across the 
north-central Plains, becoming northeasterly over eastern portions of Wyoming 
and Colorado. The uncalibrated ECENS depicts a 20-30 percent chance of 6 inches 
or more of upslope snow over portions of the Central Rockies, including the 
more populated areas along the eastern foothills of the Front Range such as 
Denver, Fort Collins, and Cheyenne. However, the uncalibrated GEFS depicts less 
than a 10 percent chance of exceeding this threshold. Given increased 
uncertainty, a slight risk of heavy snow is posted for central Colorado, 
southeast Wyoming, and the western Nebraska Panhandle, Nov 21-22.



Surface high pressure near the northern Mid-Atlantic coast is anticipated to 
steer significant Atlantic and Gulf return moisture into the central CONUS. 
Predicted mid-level troughing over the West and a surface cyclone in the lee of 
the Rockies combined with enhanced moisture supports increased chances for 
heavy precipitation across parts of the central and east-central CONUS. Various 
uncalibrated and calibrated model tools support a slight risk of heavy 
precipitation that encompasses much of the eastern Plains and Mississippi 
Valley, Upper Great Lakes region, and western portions of the Ohio and 
Tennessee Valleys, and Southeastern CONUS, Nov 21-22. The uncalibrated ECENS 
and GEFS predict 20-40 percent chances of 3-day accumulated totals (about 
1-inch) within the designated slight risk area. The GEFS (ECENS) Probabilistic 
Extremes Tools (PETs) are depicting a 20 (30) percent chance of 3-day 
precipitation totals exceeding an inch and the 85th percentile, over about the 
southern half of the designated slight risk area. Adequate Gulf moisture 
increases the chance for thunderstorms in this general region. According to the 
U.S. Drought Monitor valid on Nov 10, 85 percent of Arkansas is designed with 
D3 to D4. This wet latter half of November will be largely beneficial and bring 
much needed drought relief to the Ozarks, Middle to Lower Mississippi Valley, 
and Southern Great Plains.



0z ECENS 10-meter wind gusts (and to a lesser extent, the PETs) favor wind 
speeds of 20 knots or greater for much of the CONUS between the Rockies and the 
Appalachians, Nov 21-24. Though the designated high wind area may be overdone 
in terms of spatial coverage, the broadbrushed pattern aligns with the expected 
track of the mid-level trough, surface cyclone (with its uncertainty), and the 
associated cold front.



On Nov 24-25, colder air drawn in behind the storm system moving across the 
Central and Eastern CONUS may result in the first light freeze (32 deg F) of 
the season for northern and central sections of the Southern Plains. This is 
consistent with ECENS and GEFS temperature PET tools. According to the 
Midwestern Regional Climate Center, areas north of here have already 
experienced their first light freeze of the season. Therefore, a slight risk of 
much below normal temperatures is confined to the area denoted above from Nov 
24-25.



California and southwestern Oregon may see a brief break in the active weather 
pattern during the first half of the week-2 period. After this, most objective 
guidance including the Integrated water Vapor Transport (IVT) tools using the 
250 kg/m-s threshold, is in fairly good agreement indicating enhanced onshore 
flow into southwestern Oregon and northern California around day 11 or 12. 
Therefore, slight risks of heavy precipitation and high winds are indicated for 
this region from Nov 25-27. In addition, a slight risk of heavy snow (6+ 
inches) is posted for the higher elevations of the Klamath and Sierra Nevada 
Mountains for this same period, supported by the raw snow totals from the ECENS 
ensemble system.



Although the persistent longwave trough over the North Pacific is likely to 
result in periods of enhanced winds and precipitation to southwestern Alaska, 
hazardous thresholds are not expected to be reached.

FORECASTER: Anthony Artusa
